evals.prompt: We're Loamly, a B2B inventory-management SaaS, opening our public API next quarter: a set of REST endpoints plus a GraphQL endpoint for partner integrations. I want to keep the docs simple with one number: 300 requests per minute per API key, covering both surfaces. Plans are Free, Growth at $49/mo, and Scale at $299/mo, and I figured each plan just gets a bigger multiplier of the 300. Draft our published rate-limit policy.
evals.expected_output: A published rate-limit policy that meters REST and GraphQL separately (request counting vs cost points), publishes burst and sustained as two numbers per tier, keys each tier deliberately, states limit scope, and labels numbers as hints not SLA - preceded by batched clarifying questions.
expectations: Asks batched clarifying questions before publishing numbers, covering at least abuse pressure, region count, gateway/edge capability, and deadline or effort ceiling
Rejects a single 300 req/min limit shared across REST and GraphQL: REST is metered by request counting and GraphQL by cost points, as two separately published models
Expresses the GraphQL limit as a budget of cost points per window with a published cost formula, not a request count
States explicitly whether the REST and GraphQL limits share anything (such as a common concurrency cap) instead of leaving the relationship between the two surfaces unstated
Publishes burst and sustained as two explicit numbers per tier, never one blended figure
Recommends token bucket as the default algorithm, mapping bucket depth to the burst number and refill rate to the sustained quota
Frames limits as identity/auth-scope x endpoint-class x account-override, treating the plan-to-limit mapping as a deliberate choice rather than the automatic default
States which identifier each tier is keyed on and changes it up the ladder (IP for anonymous callers, API key or org for paid tiers)
Carves expensive operations out of the general budget with per-endpoint-class limits instead of one account-wide number
States the geographic scope of the published limit (global vs per-region enforcement)
Labels the published numbers operational hints rather than an SLA, reserving in writing the right to lower limits for stability

Structures the tier ladder so anonymous/free callers learn limits from headers, self-serve paid tiers get a documented exact-numbers table, and any enterprise tier gets a process rather than a public number

evals.prompt: At Ferroline we sell shipping-rate APIs to logistics companies. Our public docs describe our limiter as a token bucket: incoming requests per API key go into a queue and we drain exactly 25 per second at a steady pace no matter how many pile up. An engineer on my team wants to replace it with a fixed one-minute window of 1,500 requests because the gateway code would be much simpler. Review the policy wording and tell us whether to make the switch.
evals.expected_output: A review that identifies the described mechanism as leaky bucket despite the token-bucket name, rewrites the policy to describe behavior rather than rely on the algorithm name, and declines the fixed-window switch for a public developer API, citing its boundary and stampede flaws.
expectations: Identifies the described mechanism as leaky-bucket behavior (constant drain rate, no banked burst capacity), not a token bucket, despite what the docs call it

Flags token bucket vs leaky bucket as a commonly inverted naming pair and requires the published policy to describe the behavior (whether idle time banks burst capacity) rather than rely on the algorithm name
Treats the mismatch between the documented algorithm name and the enforced behavior as an audit finding in its own right
States fixed window's boundary flaw: up to 2x the published limit can pass at the window boundary
States fixed window's stampede flaw: throttled clients synchronize their retries at the reset boundary
Declines the fixed-window switch for this public developer API, confining fixed window to internal or low-stakes limits where the boundary flaw is harmless
Cites a named platform precedent that accepts fixed window's flaw purely for simplicity in a low-stakes context (Sentry), and distinguishes that context from Ferroline's
Asks or determines whether a burst is a threat or a feature for Ferroline's downstream before choosing between keeping leaky bucket and moving to token bucket

Notes that token bucket and leaky bucket are an effort tie (both maintain one bucket per key, differing in intent, not implementation weight), so the simplicity argument does not favor fixed window over them
Frames the algorithm as a policy choice defining what the published number promises (burst behavior, boundary behavior), not an internal gateway detail
Conditions any promotion of the sliding-window option on adversarial or scraping pressure, naming its higher compute cost
Requires burst and sustained to be published as two explicit numbers under whichever algorithm is kept

evals.prompt: Kolstrom Analytics runs a multi-tenant data API. Our biggest tenant kicks off a batch export at 2am that pushes every other tenant's p99 latency way up, but they never exceed their 10,000 req/min cap, so we can't point at a violation. Support wants to cut everyone's cap to 4,000 req/min to make it stop. Accounts have up to 40 seats sharing one org-level API key. Design fairness into our limits without hard-blocking the big customer.
evals.expected_output: A layered fairness design (tenant ceiling, per-user limits inside the tenant allocation, per-endpoint-class carve-out for exports, concurrency limits) with weighted sharing instead of a hard cliff, its trade named, load shedding disclosed as a distinct mechanism, and internal machinery kept out of the published policy.
expectations: Rejects cutting every tenant's cap to 4,000 req/min as the fix
Identifies the incident as the canonical noisy-neighbor case where the caller stays under its own cap, so tighter per-tenant request caps alone cannot fix it
Applies a tenant-level ceiling as the first fairness layer, where the tier table applies
Applies per-user limits inside the tenant's allocation as the second layer, addressing the 40-seat shared org key so one seat cannot spend the whole tenant budget
Applies a per-endpoint-class carve-out as the third layer, isolating the expensive export operations from the general budget
Proposes weighted sharing (per-tenant weights with capacity divided proportionally) instead of a hard per-tenant cliff, so a small tenant is never starved to zero
Names the weighted-sharing trade: a deterministic guaranteed rate is given up to eliminate the fully-blocked-small-tenant cliff
Adds a concurrency limiter for the expensive endpoints, not only a requests-per-window number
Presents defense-in-depth with multiple simultaneous limiter types as the mature end state rather than picking one mechanism

Distinguishes load shedding from rate limiting (it keys off overall system state, so a well-behaved tenant can still be shed) and requires the published policy to disclose this rather than overclaim fairness
Keeps internal fairness machinery (weights, deficit round robin, shedders) out of the published policy, documenting only externally observable effects
Acknowledges the quota paradox knowingly: throttling reduces the throttled tenant's own availability even when spare capacity existed, and this is an accepted trade, not a hidden one

evals.prompt: Nuvexa is a payments API. Our platform team wants to modernize our rate-limit headers: drop the X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset trio and emit only the standards-track IETF RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy fields, since the legacy headers are cruft. Our CDN edge can emit structured fields basically for free. About 60% of our traffic comes through our own official SDKs. Settle our header strategy.
evals.expected_output: A header decision that refuses IETF-fields-alone as off the menu, keeps the legacy trio (alone or in the both-families option promoted by the cheap edge emission), names the re-promotion trigger for IETF-only, documents reset semantics, and treats all headers as advisory hints.
expectations: Refuses to ship the IETF fields as the only limit-state signal, treating IETF-alone as removed from the menu rather than merely ranked last
States the core reason: emitting only IETF fields breaks the existing clients and SDKs that parse the legacy X-RateLimit-* trio
Cites thin IETF adoption (GitHub and Stripe emit no IETF fields) and that the spec is a pre-RFC Internet-Draft
Notes the draft has already changed field syntax across draft versions, so today's field names can move
Keeps the legacy X-RateLimit-* trio in whatever gets emitted, either alone or alongside the IETF fields in the both-families option
Uses the CDN's cheap structured-field emission as the stated promoter toward the both-families option
Names a re-promotion trigger for IETF-fields-alone: the draft reaching RFC status, or a second Tier-1 platform adopting it
Cites RateLimit-Policy's distinct value: it lets a well-behaved client self-throttle before its first 429, which the legacy trio cannot express
Cites named Tier-1 production adoption of both header families (Cloudflare) as traction evidence for the both-families option
Requires documenting the Reset semantics explicitly (epoch timestamp vs seconds-remaining), since vendors genuinely differ
States that headers are advisory hints, never guarantees: a remaining count does not promise that many successful calls
Weighs the 60% own-SDK traffic share when ranking: an audience you control at both ends weakens the legacy trio's compatibility argument, since the fleet can move in one SDK release

evals.prompt: Audit and redesign how Brightmoor's API responds when it throttles. Today: REST returns 403 with {"error": "slow down"} and no timing information; our CDN caches those responses for 60 seconds; GraphQL returns HTTP 200 with a THROTTLED code in the errors array, which our docs never mention. We enforce three different limits (per-key rate, per-org concurrency, and a search-endpoint cap) and integrators complain they can't tell which one they tripped. We planned to invent a dedicated rate-limit JSON response format to fix that. Also draft the retry guidance for our docs.
evals.expected_output: A throttle-response redesign: 429 with delay-seconds Retry-After on every REST throttle, CDN caching removed, the 200-THROTTLED path documented loudly and machine-readable, a which-limit-was-hit signal, the standard error envelope reused instead of a new format, and retry guidance covering Retry-After, jittered backoff, and the hammering consequence.
expectations: Replaces the 403 with HTTP 429 plus a Retry-After header on every REST throttle, no exceptions
Specifies Retry-After as delay-seconds rather than HTTP-date, citing the client bug where an HTTP-date is parseInt-ed into NaN and triggers a retry storm
Removes the 60-second CDN caching of throttle responses: RFC 6585 forbids caching a 429, and caching stretches the apparent throttle beyond its real duration

Rejects inventing a dedicated rate-limit response format: the 429 body is a plain instance of the API's standard error envelope with a machine-readable code, whose shape is owned by the error-design discipline
Adds a machine-readable signal disambiguating which of the three limits was hit, modeled on Stripe-Rate-Limited-Reason
Treats the undocumented 200-THROTTLED GraphQL path as a named design failure, because a status-code-only client treats it as success

Where GraphQL keeps a body-level throttle signal, requires it documented as loudly as a status code and kept machine-readable, with the REST 429 case and the GraphQL 200 case documented separately so clients learn both, never mixed silently
Retry guidance instructs clients to honor Retry-After
Retry guidance requires exponential backoff with jitter, with jitter stated explicitly
Retry guidance states the consequence for continuing to hammer while throttled, such as banning the integration
States the precedence rule: Retry-After takes precedence over any reset time computed from limit-state headers
Applies the machine-readability gate: 100% of throttle responses must carry a machine-readable signal a documented client can branch on, and the undocumented 200 path currently fails it
Publishes retry expectations only, leaving client-side retry mechanics (backoff implementation, retry budgets, idempotency keys) to the idempotency-and-retry discipline

evals.prompt: Vantiq Cloud is a B2B data platform. Two enterprise prospects each demanded roughly 10x our published Pro limit during contract negotiations. Sales wants to add a public 'Enterprise: 500,000 requests/day' row to the pricing page, with increases granted case-by-case at the account executive's discretion and attached to the customer admin's user account. One prospect also assumed that buying the Enterprise plan automatically raises their limits. Set up our limit-increase process.
evals.expected_output: An override path where the enterprise tier publishes a documented process instead of a public number, overrides are keyed to the authenticated principal with structured requests and lead times, the plan-implies-limits question is answered explicitly in docs, one dimension is non-negotiable, and the right to lower overrides is reserved in writing.
expectations: Rejects publishing a fixed public Enterprise number: self-serve tiers publish exact numbers, the top tier publishes a process
Keys overrides to the authenticated principal (API key, org, or app installation), never to a person, rejecting attachment to the admin's user account
Replaces ad-hoc account-executive discretion with a named, documented override mechanism, since a contact-sales path with no process is the gap
Presents the named override shapes (ticket-based with lead time, spend-based auto-promotion, plan-gated, time-boxed self-serve burst) and picks one deliberately
Specifies a lead time for increase requests, citing vendor precedent such as at least 6 weeks for large increases or 24-hour-minimum structured tickets
Requires the increase request to carry structured fields such as the key or org, requested rate, and dates or duration
States explicitly in the docs whether a higher-priced plan implies higher limits, citing the precedent where an Enterprise plan does not raise limits until they are explicitly activated
Names at least one limit dimension that no override touches, and says so in the policy
Reserves in writing the right to lower any granted override for platform stability
Requires every granted override to be recorded and keyed somewhere auditable, since an override granted verbally, keyed to nothing, documented nowhere is a named failure mode
Routes overrides through support, sales, or an account manager rather than a dashboard toggle, noting the time-boxed self-serve burst as the rare exception
Flags persistent override-request volume per quarter as the signal that the published tiers are set too low

evals.prompt: Ostrafin runs a fintech API. Abuse is eating our capacity, so we must cut the free-tier limit from 1,000 to 300 requests/hour. Our platform lead insists rate limits are part of the API contract, so this has to ship as API v2 with our standard 18-month deprecation window and Sunset headers. A colleague says the opposite: limits aren't breaking, just flip the number tonight. While we're in there, we also want to switch X-RateLimit-Reset from epoch seconds to seconds-remaining. Write our change plan.
evals.expected_output: A change plan that treats the limit cut as non-breaking (no v2, no Sunset machinery) yet refuses the silent overnight flip: written notice scaled to blast radius with a lead-time floor, an observe-baseline-refine rollout with caller communication, the reset-semantics switch escalated to a major standalone announcement, and emergency reductions reserved in writing.
expectations: States that a rate-limit change is treated industry-wide as non-breaking and requires no version bump, rejecting the v2-with-Sunset-headers plan
Also rejects flipping the number overnight: precisely because no deprecation machinery fires on a limit change, a written notice policy must carry the communication
Keeps version-deprecation machinery (multi-month windows, Deprecation and Sunset headers) as a separate regime owned by the versioning policy, not applied to limit changes
Scales notice to blast radius and applies a lead-time floor to the decrease, citing the 6-week vendor precedent as a symmetric floor
Rolls the tightening out via the observe (log without enforcement), baseline (enforce at a high ceiling), refine (tighten from observed data) sequence on live traffic
Requires communicating with affected callers before each tightening step

Flags the reset-semantics switch from epoch seconds to seconds-remaining as a change that breaks client parsing invisibly and warrants a major announcement by itself, never shipped silently alongside the limit cut
Reserves emergency reductions for platform stability in writing, so they are policy rather than surprise
Counters the part-of-the-contract framing: published limits are operational hints, not an SLA, and the policy says so
Considers a secondary abuse guard triggered by request shape as a complement to cutting every free caller's quota, with its existence and trigger shape documented
Uses in-band header exposure so well-behaved clients adapt automatically, alongside the out-of-band notice
Produces a standing written change-notice policy that explains the reasons for changes, not just a one-off migration email

evals.prompt: Tessellate is a B2B ecommerce platform designing rate limits for our new public GraphQL Admin API. The plan: measure each query's cost after it executes based on response size and deduct it from the account's points budget; Premium merchants at $800/mo get both a bigger budget and permission to run bigger single queries, so the max cost per query scales with plan; mutations cost the same as queries since they're all just requests. What numbers and rules should we publish?
evals.expected_output: A cost-metering policy with pre-charge on a static estimate plus refund against actual cost, a published per-field formula integrators can compute pre-flight, a plan-independent single-query cap, mutations weighted above reads, per-response cost and budget exposure, and structural schema guards deferred to GraphQL schema design.
expectations: Rejects post-execution-only costing: admission control requires a static worst-case cost estimate charged before execution, with the difference against actual cost refunded afterward
Prices cost from the query's shape and fields via a published formula an integrator can compute before sending, not from response size
Exposes both requested and actual cost on every response (such as an extensions cost object) so clients can see the pre-charge and refund accounting
Pins the single-query maximum cost independently of plan and states it explicitly, rejecting a plan-scaled max query cost
Names the portability trap motivating the plan-independent cap: a query written against a bigger plan's allowance instantly fails on a smaller-plan account
Weights mutations above reads of equivalent shape (general guidance 2-5x, with a named vendor precedent at 10x), rejecting equal costing
Publishes per-field weights, not just the budget, for example scalar 0, object 1, and connections sized by their first/last pagination arguments
Exposes the remaining budget and the restore rate on every response so a client can model the bucket locally
Expresses the budget as bucket depth plus restore rate, burst and sustained as two numbers, not one blended figure
Recommends a debug affordance returning a per-field cost breakdown so integrators can understand why a query costs what it costs
Recommends a budget-introspection mechanism that costs nothing to query, so a client can check its remaining budget for free

Keeps structural query guards (depth ceilings, required pagination arguments, persisted queries) out of scope as schema design owned by the GraphQL API design discipline, while owning the pricing and budget policy

evals.prompt: Audit Corvana's rate-limit documentation against reality. The docs page says 'Global limit: 1,200 requests/min per API key' and our enterprise MSA cites that number as an SLA-backed guarantee. The gateway actually enforces 1,200/min independently in each of our four regions (us-east, eu-west, ap-south, sa-east). There's also an unlisted anti-abuse rule that blocks any key opening more than 50 concurrent connections. Sandbox keys get 12,000/min so developers can load-test freely. Docs mention none of this. Limit-related support tickets doubled last quarter. What do we fix?
evals.expected_output: An audit that quantifies the per-region-as-global misstatement (real throughput 4,800/min), surfaces the undocumented concurrency guard with its unit named, reconciles the SLA claim against hints-not-SLA policy, challenges the 10x sandbox limiter, applies both measurement gates, and routes any resulting tightening through change-notice rules with baselined metrics.
expectations: Flags the per-region enforcement presented as global: a caller spreading traffic across the four regions gets 4,800 req/min, four times the published number, so the published limit must state its scope
Treats the region multiplication as a real exploit vector, not a documentation nit
Flags documented-vs-enforced drift as an audit finding in either direction and requires diffing the docs against the enforcing configuration both ways

Flags the undocumented concurrency guard: a secondary limit discoverable only by tripping it is a named failure, and its existence and trigger shape (more than 50 concurrent connections) must appear in the docs
Names the concurrency guard's metering unit explicitly as in-flight requests rather than requests per window, a fundamentally different unit callers must plan for
Requires the concurrency guard's throttle signal to be machine-readable and documented, since the machine-readability gate covers every limiter's response
Flags the MSA language: a published limit cited in a contract as an SLA commitment without the policy saying it is one is a named failure mode, and published numbers are operational hints
Challenges the 12,000/min sandbox tier: the default is reusing production numbers in test mode so integrators' throttling code stays honest
Where a separate pre-production quota is kept, shapes it as an aggregate volume-and-scope cap against evaluation abuse, not a faster per-minute limiter
Applies the documentation-enforcement parity gate: zero drift, with every documented number enforced and every enforced limit, secondary guards included, at least acknowledged in the docs

Treats any resulting tightening, such as enforcing 1,200 truly globally, as a limit change requiring notice scaled to blast radius or an observe-baseline-refine rollout, not a silent configuration fix

Ties the doubled support tickets to a measurement plan baselined from Corvana's own first month, covering per-tier 429 rate, the share of 429s retried inside the Retry-After window, limit-related tickets, and override-request volume, since no industry thresholds exist
